s0302.literal: At the time wishing to broaden agriculture, Xi submitted a memorial saying: he was transferred to assistant editorial director, compiled the Jin History annals and the ten treatises, was transferred to erudite, and his editorial duties remained as before.
s0302.idiomatic: When the court wanted to promote farming, Shu Xi offered policy advice; he was then made assistant director of composition, tasked with drafting the dynastic annals and ten monographs of the Jin History, promoted to academician, and kept his editorial post.

s0303.literal: In the beginning, a man of Ji commandery named Bu Zhun robbed open the tomb of King Xiang of Wei, or some say the mound of King Ai of An, and obtained several cartloads of bamboo documents.
s0303.idiomatic: Earlier, Bu Zhun of Ji commandery broke into the tomb of King Xiang of Wei—some identify it as the burial of King Ai of An—and hauled out dozens of cartloads of bamboo texts.

s0304.literal: Among them the Bamboo Annals in thirteen sections records from Xia down to King You of Zhou destroyed by the Dog Rong, joins events to it, the three houses divided Jin, and still narrates Wei affairs down to the twentieth year of King Ai.
s0304.idiomatic: Its Bamboo Annals, in thirteen fascicles, runs from the Xia down through King You of Zhou, overrun by the Dog Rong, carries the story into the partition among the three great houses, and continues Wei history to the twentieth year of King Ai.

s0305.literal: It was broadly the historical writings of the state of Wei; in large outline they largely corresponded with the Spring and Autumn Annals.
s0305.idiomatic: These were essentially Wei state annals that, in the main, align closely with the Spring and Autumn.

s0306.literal: Among them where classic and commentary greatly differed, then it said the Xia calendar had more years than the Yin.
s0306.idiomatic: Where its record diverges sharply from received classics, it claims the Xia reign count exceeds that of the Shang.

s0307.literal: Yi interfered with Qi's position; Qi killed him.
s0307.idiomatic: Yi usurped Qi's throne; Qi had him killed.

s0309.idiomatic: King Wen Ding put Ji Li to death.

s0310.literal: From the Zhou receiving the mandate down to King Mu was one hundred years; it is not that King Mu's lifespan was one hundred years.
s0310.idiomatic: It counts a century from Zhou's receipt of the mandate to King Mu—not a claim that King Mu lived a hundred years.

s0311.literal: After King You had perished, there was Gong Bo He who acted in the Son of Heaven's affairs; it was not the two ministers' joint rule called 'harmony.'
s0311.idiomatic: After King You fell, Gong Bo He held the regency; this is not the 'joint harmony' regency of two ministers in received tradition.

s0312.literal: Its Changes Classic in two sections was the same as the Zhou Changes upper and lower classics.
s0312.idiomatic: Its two-part Changes matches the upper and lower wings of the Zhou Changes.

s0313.literal: The Changes of Yin and Yang Hexagrams in two sections was largely the same as the Zhou Changes, but the oracle texts differed.
s0313.idiomatic: The two scrolls of Yin-Yang line statements largely parallel the Zhou Changes, though the line texts diverge.

s0314.literal: The Changes Classic beneath the Hexagrams in one piece resembled Explaining the Hexagrams but differed.
s0314.idiomatic: One scroll of sub-hexagram commentary resembles the Explaining the Hexagrams yet is not identical.

s0315.literal: Gongsun Duan in two sections: Gongsun Duan and Shao Zhi discussed the Changes.
s0315.idiomatic: Two scrolls titled Gongsun Duan record a dialogue on the Changes between Gongsun Duan and Shao Zhi.

s0316.literal: Discourses of the States in three sections spoke of Chu and Jin affairs.
s0316.idiomatic: A three-part Discourses of the States treats events in Chu and Jin.

s0317.literal: The Names in three sections resembled the Record of Rites, and also resembled the Erya and the Analects.
s0317.idiomatic: A three-part Names recalls both the Record of Rites and compendia in the vein of the Erya and Analects.

s0318.literal: Shichun in one piece wrote the various divinations of the Zuo Tradition; 'Shichun' seems to be the name of the person who made the book.
s0318.idiomatic: Shichun collects the Zuo Tradition's divination episodes; the title probably preserves the compiler's name.

s0319.literal: Trivial Sayings in eleven sections was the book of the various states' dream divinations, prodigies, and physiognomy.
s0319.idiomatic: Eleven fascicles of Trivial Sayings compile dream omens, anomalies, and physiognomy lore from many states.

s0320.literal: Liangqiu Zang in one piece first narrated the generations of Wei, next spoke of hill-hoard gold and jade matters.
s0320.idiomatic: Liangqiu Zang opens with Wei reign chronology, then turns to buried treasure in hill vaults.

s0321.literal: Corded-arrow Writings in two sections discussed the method of corded-arrow shooting.
s0321.idiomatic: Two scrolls on corded-arrow archery spell out the technique.

s0322.literal: Shengfeng in one piece was what emperors enfeoffed.

s0323.literal: Great Calendar in two sections was of the kind of Master Zou discoursing on heaven.
s0323.idiomatic: Great Calendar, in two parts, belongs with cosmological writings in the tradition of Zou Yan.

s0324.literal: Tradition of King Mu of Zhou in five sections spoke of King Mu of Zhou roaming the four seas, seeing Di Tai and the Queen Mother of the West.
s0324.idiomatic: Five scrolls of the King Mu tradition describe his tour of the realm and meetings with Di Tai and the Queen Mother of the West.

s0325.literal: Illustrated Poems in one piece belonged to the kind of painted eulogies.
s0325.idiomatic: Illustrated Poems is a gallery-style verse cycle with captions.

s0326.literal: Also miscellaneous writings nineteen pieces: Zhou Field-allotment Law, Zhou Documents, Discussing Chu Affairs, Affair of the Death of King Mu of Zhou's Beautiful Lady Sheng Ji.
s0326.idiomatic: Another nineteen miscellaneous works include Zhou field law, Zhou state papers, essays on Chu, and the death of King Mu's consort Sheng Ji.

s0327.literal: In all seventy-five sections; seven bamboo bundles were broken, their titles not known.
s0327.idiomatic: Seventy-five titles survive in all; seven damaged bundles could not be identified.

s0328.literal: From the tomb they also obtained one bronze sword, length two chi five cun.
s0328.idiomatic: The diggers also pulled out a bronze sword two and a half feet long.

s0329.literal: The lacquer writing was all tadpole characters.
s0329.idiomatic: The lacquered slips were all in tadpole seal script.

s0330.literal: At first those who opened the tomb burned slips to shine and take treasures; when officials collected them, many were burnt slips and broken slips; the text being already incomplete, they could no longer arrange the order.
s0330.idiomatic: Looters first torched slips for light while plundering treasure, so when officials recovered the haul much was charred or snapped; the text was too fragmentary to restore original order.

s0331.literal: Emperor Wu handed the documents to the Palace Library to collate sequence, investigate point and return, and write them in current script.
s0331.idiomatic: Emperor Wu entrusted the slips to the imperial library for collation, interpretation, and transcription into regular script.

s0332.literal: Xi while in the composition post was able to view the bamboo documents; following doubts he split and explained them; all had reasoned verification.
s0332.idiomatic: As an editorial scribe, Shu Xi could study the cache and produced well-argued clarifications wherever the text was obscure.

s0333.literal: He was promoted to gentleman of the Secretariat.
s0333.idiomatic: He rose to secretary in the imperial secretariat.

s0334.literal: Emperor Wu once asked Zhi Yu the meaning of the third-day curved-water gathering; Yu replied: 'In the time of Han Zhangdi, Pingyuan Xu Zhao on the third of the third month bore three daughters; by the third day all had died; the villagers thought it strange, then led them to the water's edge to wash and exorcise; therefore by the water they floated goblets; its meaning began here.'
s0334.idiomatic: Emperor Wu once asked Zhi Yu why courtiers held the spring outing with floating cups along a winding channel. Zhi Yu traced it to Han Zhangdi's reign, when Xu Zhao of Pingyuan bore triplets on the third day of the third month and lost all three by the feast day; neighbors led the family to the river for purification, then set cups adrift on the current—so the custom began, he said.

s0335.literal: The emperor said: 'If it must be as you have spoken, then it is not a good affair.'
s0335.idiomatic: The emperor replied, 'If that origin is true, the rite rests on ill omen, not merit.'

s0336.literal: Xi stepped forward and said: 'Yu is a young student, not sufficient to know; your servant begs to speak of it.'
s0336.idiomatic: Shu Xi interjected: 'Zhi Yu is too junior to settle this; allow me to answer.'

s0337.literal: Anciently the Duke of Zhou completed Luoyi; by flowing water he floated wine; therefore a lost poem says: "Feather goblets follow the waves."
s0337.idiomatic: When the Duke of Zhou finished Luoyang, he already drifted cups on a winding stream—a lost ode speaks of goblets riding the ripples.

s0338.literal: Also King Zhao of Qin on the third day set wine at the river bend, saw a golden man presenting a sword from the heart of the water, saying: 'Order you, lord, to control Western Xia.'
s0338.idiomatic: King Zhao of Qin likewise feasted by a bend on the third day, saw a golden figure offer a sword from midstream, and heard the pledge that the ruler would master the western regions.

s0339.literal: Then he hegemoned the feudal lords; because of this it was established as curved water.
s0339.idiomatic: He went on to lord it over the lords, and the winding-stream banquet became a precedent for power.

s0340.literal: The two Han continued it; all were grand gatherings.
s0340.idiomatic: Both Western and Eastern Han kept the custom, always as splendid court festivals.

s0341.literal: The emperor was greatly pleased and bestowed on Xi fifty jin of gold.
s0341.idiomatic: Delighted, the emperor awarded Shu Xi fifty jin of gold.

s0342.literal: At the time someone below Songgao Mountain obtained one bamboo slip; on it two lines of tadpole writing; they passed it around to show one another; none knew it.
s0342.idiomatic: Someone then found a single slip below Mount Song with two lines of tadpole script; it circulated among scholars, but no one could read it.

s0343.literal: Minister of Works Zhang Hua used it to ask Xi; Xi said: 'This is the tomb-strategy text from Emperor Ming of Han's Xianjie mausoleum.'
s0343.idiomatic: Zhang Hua, as minister of works, showed it to Shu Xi, who identified it as a burial inscription from Emperor Ming's Xianjie tomb.

s0344.literal: Inspection verified it was so; people of the time submitted to his broad learning.
s0344.idiomatic: Archives confirmed his reading, and contemporaries marveled at his erudition.

s0345.literal: Prince Zhao Lun was chancellor of state and requested him to be secretary in the headquarters.
s0345.idiomatic: When Prince Zhao Lun served as chief minister, he tried to appoint Shu Xi chief secretary of his staff.

s0346.literal: Xi declined citing illness, resigned and returned, and taught disciples.
s0346.idiomatic: Shu Xi pleaded illness, went home, and taught private students.

s0347.literal: He died at forty; the market ward of Yuancheng city for him ceased work; disciples and old friends erected a stele beside the tomb.
s0347.idiomatic: He died at forty; trades in Yuancheng's market suspended business in mourning; pupils and friends set up a stone by his grave.

s0348.literal: Xi's talents and learning broadly penetrated; what he wrote—Records of Worthies of the Three Weis, Comprehensive Record of Seven Dynasties, Jin Annals and Treatises—met turmoil and was lost.
s0348.idiomatic: Shu Xi was encyclopedic, but his Records of Wei Notables, Seven Dynasties Digest, and drafts of the Jin annals and monographs perished in the wars.

s0349.literal: His Comprehensive Discussion of the Five Classics, Notes for Opening the Dark, Poems to Repair the Lost, and collected writings several tens of chapters moved in the world.
s0349.idiomatic: His Five Classics synthesis, primer notes, supplement to the lost odes, and collected essays—several dozen scrolls—did circulate.

s0351.literal: Wang Jie, style Zuyou, was a man of Yishi in Hedong, tenth-generation descendant of Han capital intendant Wang Zun.
s0351.idiomatic: Wang Jie, courtesy Zuyou, came from Yishi in Hedong and was the tenth-generation heir of Wang Zun, metropolitan governor under Han.

s0352.literal: His father Wei, for generations cultivated Confucian and historical learning.
s0352.idiomatic: His father Wang Wei came from a long line of Confucian historians.

s0353.literal: Wei central army supervisor Cao Xi made the Treatise on Utmost Impartiality; Wei praised it and wrote the Treatise on Utmost Pivot; its phrasing and meaning were very fine.
s0353.idiomatic: When Cao Xi, central army supervisor under Wei, wrote On Utmost Fairness, Wang Wei admired it and replied with On the Ultimate Pivot—an essay of rare polish.

s0354.literal: His office reached chancellor of the marquisate of Xiayang.
s0354.idiomatic: He rose to magistrate-chancellor of the Xiayang marquisate.

s0355.literal: Jie in youth lost his father; grief destroyed beyond the rites; villagers all sighed: 'The Wang clan has a son!'
s0355.idiomatic: Wang Jie lost his father young and mourned past what ritual prescribed; neighbors exclaimed that the Wangs had raised a worthy heir.

s0356.literal: Liu Yuan of Bohai was Hedong grand warden; he loved the strange and took displaying talent as his task.
s0356.idiomatic: Liu Yuan of Bohai, as Hedong governor, cultivated odd talents and made a point of promoting them.

s0357.literal: Feng Shou of the same commandery tested the classics to become a gentleman; over seventy; he recommended Jie to Yuan, saying: 'If fine steeds do not have the reins gathered, then it is not Zaofu's stable.'
s0357.idiomatic: Feng Shou of the same commandery, a classics graduate in his seventies, urged Liu Yuan: 'A team unhitched is no chariot for Zaofu.'

s0358.literal: If the bright moon does not cast flowing light, then it is not in the Marquis of Sui's palm.
s0358.idiomatic: A moonbeam withheld is no pearl in the Marquis of Sui's hand.

s0359.literal: I humbly consider that the enlightened prefect embraces the virtue of the yellow center, shines the brightness of layered li, seeks worthies and the able, and in small things has no oversight; therefore this lowly old man wishes to present what he knows.
s0359.idiomatic: Your honor unites inner strength with outward clarity, misses no talent however slight, so this aged subject ventures a name you should hear.

s0360.literal: Privately I see recluse Wang Jie, outstanding and sharp, at thirteen orphaned; in mourning he exhausted the rites; learning—on passing the eyes he knew; principles—touching categories he lengthened; this is the fine flavor of the jade handle, the emblematic plan for ordering the age.
s0360.idiomatic: The recluse Wang Jie is precocious and keen: orphaned at thirteen yet scrupulous in mourning, he reads once and retains, and extends doctrine by analogy—true metal for the state's tripod, a design for governing the age.

s0361.literal: Not worrying that the dark-haired masses will not awaken; privately I rejoice that spring's blossoms catch the season.
s0361.idiomatic: I do not fear the people will stay blind to him; I rejoice that spring has brought its bloom in good time.

s0362.literal: Yuan immediately with ritual summoned him; Jie did not accept.
s0362.idiomatic: Liu Yuan at once sent a formal summons; Wang Jie declined.

s0363.literal: Yuan then called him to a meeting and said: 'Do you wish to admire the height of fat reclusion?'
s0363.idiomatic: Liu Yuan then had him brought in and asked whether he meant to rival the loftiest hermits.

s0364.literal: He replied: 'Jie's fate is thin in blessing; young orphaned and without brothers; mother old, illness heavy; therefore I have no heart to be a clerk.'
s0364.idiomatic: Wang Jie answered that his life had been starved of fortune—orphaned early, brotherless, with an aged mother gravely ill—so office held no appeal.

s0365.literal: When his mother ended, he wasted from grief until bones stood; he dwelt by the tomb for years, thoroughly read the many books, and mostly produced divergent interpretations.
s0365.idiomatic: After she died he wasted to the bone and lived at the graveside for years, reading widely and often dissenting from received glosses.

s0366.literal: His nature was simple and direct; he did not cultivate vulgar deportment; great clans of the village mostly could not treat him well; only Pei Wei elegantly knew him.
s0366.idiomatic: Plain and blunt, he scorned small-town polish, so local grandees disliked him—only Pei Wei truly understood him.

s0367.literal: Pingyang grand warden Liu Dan, scattered-cavalry attendant Pei Xia, and supervisor of the masters of writing Deng You all were friendly with Jie.
s0367.idiomatic: Liu Dan, governor of Pingyang, attendant Pei Xia, and chief minister Deng You all counted him a friend.

s0368.literal: Later he became the county's principal clerk, welcomed Grand Warden Wen Yu; Yu thought him strange, transferred him to merit clerk.
s0368.idiomatic: He later served as county recorder, impressed Governor Wen Yu on his arrival, and was moved to merit secretary.

s0369.literal: The province summoned him as Pingyang staff clerk.
s0369.idiomatic: The provincial authorities then named him an aide on the Pingyang staff.

s0370.literal: At the time Taishan Yang Liang was Pingyang grand warden; he recommended him to metropolitan commandant Wang Kan; he issued supplement as capital-bandits clerk.
s0370.idiomatic: When Yang Liang of Taishan governed Pingyang, he recommended Wang Jie to metropolitan commandant Wang Kan, who appointed him to the capital crimes section.

s0371.literal: At the beginning of Yongning, he was recommended as cultivated talent.
s0371.idiomatic: In the first year of Yongning he was nominated as a recommended scholar.

s0372.literal: His friend Pan Tao of Yingchuan sent Jie a letter saying: 'Zhi Yu and Bian Xuanren both say your foot ought to harmonize the cauldron's taste—can you have nothing with which to answer for cultivated-talent conduct?'
s0372.idiomatic: His friend Pan Tao wrote that Zhi Yu and Bian Xuanren expected him for high office—how could he ignore a summons to the cultivated-talent examination?

s0373.literal: Jie answered in a letter: 'Now the generation's way is mutually lost; we are about to arrive at stripping chaos; while knowing wise men seal mouth and sheathe brush, disaster daily deepens like fire on the great plain—can it be saved?'
s0373.idiomatic: Wang Jie replied that morals were collapsing toward outright pillage while thinkers sealed their lips; calamity spread like a prairie fire—what hope remained?

s0374.literal: It is not for glory this conduct; I wish to exhaust stating what I have seen, hoping there may be awakening.
s0374.idiomatic: He went not for glory but to speak his mind in the faint hope of waking the court.

s0375.literal: That year the three kings' righteous uprising; Emperor Hui restored the throne; because the state had a great celebration, all cultivated talents and filially recommended in the realm were each not tested; Jie took this as regret.
s0375.idiomatic: That year the coalition of three princes restored Emperor Hui and proclaimed a general amnesty that waived examinations for every nominated scholar; Wang Jie resented missing his chance to argue policy.

s0376.literal: He was appointed gentleman of the center and supplemented as marshal to the general who subdues barbarians.
s0376.idiomatic: He was named palace gentleman and adjunct marshal to the general who pacifies foreign foes.

s0377.literal: At the Dangyin affair, attendant-in-ordinary Xi Shao was harmed by mutinous soldiers; Jie argued: 'When one plots another's army, when the army is defeated then die for it.'
s0377.idiomatic: After Xi Shao died under rebel blades at Dangyin, Wang Jie argued that whoever shares command must share defeat.

s0378.literal: When one plots another's state, when the state is in peril then perish for it; it is the ancient way.
s0378.idiomatic: Who shares responsibility for the realm must answer with his life when the realm totters—that was the classical rule.

s0379.literal: At the Dangyin affair the hundred officials fled north; only Xi Shao kept his post encountering the not-way; he can be called a minister; also he can be called a painful record.
s0379.idiomatic: At Dangyin the court scattered in panic while Xi Shao alone held his ground against lawless troops—true ministerial fidelity and a tragedy worth recording.

s0380.literal: Now east of the mountains is about to raise a great movement; it is fitting to clarify high integrity in order to command the realm.
s0380.idiomatic: With the eastern hosts readying a major campaign, the throne should exalt steadfast loyalty to rally the empire.

s0381.literal: According to the Spring and Autumn's meaning of honoring the threefold accumulation of merit, add to Shao the reward of laying down life; then far and near will turn to the wind; none will dare not be solemn.
s0381.idiomatic: Citing the Annals' praise of cumulative merit, he urged posthumous honors for Xi Shao's martyrdom so every quarter would heed the lesson.

s0383.literal: Prince Yong of Hejian wished to move the imperial carriage to Chang'an; he differed with east of the passes; because Jie was Chengdu Prince's assistant, he found it difficult; he memorialized to transfer him to chancellor of the duke of Linfen.
s0383.idiomatic: Prince Yong of Hejian, planning to shift the court to Chang'an against the eastern alliance, sidelined Chengdu Prince's aide Wang Jie by transferring him, on memorial, to chancellor of the duke of Linfen.

s0384.literal: When Prince of East Sea Yue led the feudal lords to attack Yong, supervisor of the masters of writing Wang Kan headed the mobile headquarters; upward he requested Jie supplement as gentleman of the palace section of the masters of writing; before he arrived he died, age thirty-nine.
s0384.idiomatic: When Prince Yue of the Eastern Sea marched against Yong, chief minister Wang Kan, commanding the field secretariat, tried to add Wang Jie as a palace-section secretary—Wang Jie died at thirty-nine before he could report.

s0385.literal: Though Jie's learning was broadly penetrating, he especially mastered the Rites and the commentaries.
s0385.idiomatic: Erudite as he was, Wang Jie's deepest expertise lay in the ritual canon and its exegetical traditions.

s0386.literal: He often said the Zuo Tradition's phrasing and meaning are rich; it is its own book; it does not chiefly act to issue the classic.
s0386.idiomatic: He held that the Zuo narrative is self-sufficient literature rather than a mere gloss on the Spring and Autumn.

s0387.literal: The Gongyang attaches to the classic and sets commentary; what the classic does not write, the commentary does not recklessly begin; with regard to text it is economical; for penetrating the classic it is long.
s0387.idiomatic: Gongyang, by contrast, hews to the classic: it never invents episodes the classic omits—spare in diction yet superior for unlocking the core text.

s0388.literal: Rencheng He Xiu's exegesis is very detailed, yet demotes Zhou and kings Lu—the great outline is contrary and obstructive; moreover his aim was to penetrate Gongyang, yet often in turn makes Gongyang's diseases.
s0388.idiomatic: He Xiu of Rencheng is exhaustive yet demotes Zhou and elevates Lu, skewing the larger scheme; even while mastering Gongyang he often reproduces its faults.

s0389.literal: Jie therefore again annotated the Gongyang Spring and Autumn; much had new meanings.
s0389.idiomatic: Wang Jie therefore re-annotated the Gongyang edition, offering many fresh readings.

s0390.literal: At the time secretariat assistant Wei Heng was examining and correcting the Ji tomb documents; not finished when he encountered disaster.
s0390.idiomatic: While secretariat aide Wei Heng was still collating the tomb texts, he perished in the violence.

s0391.literal: Assistant editorial director Shu Xi narrated and completed it; matters often verified divergent meanings.
s0391.idiomatic: Assistant director Shu Xi finished the project, often adjudicating disputed passages.

s0392.literal: At the time Donglai grand warden Wang Tingjian of Chenliu disputed it; he also had evidence.
s0392.idiomatic: Wang Tingjian of Chenliu, governor of Donglai, challenged the reconstruction with documentation of his own.

s0393.literal: Xi again explained the dispute; but Tingjian had already died.
s0393.idiomatic: Shu Xi rebutted him, yet Wang Tingjian died before the debate closed.

s0394.literal: Scattered-cavalry attendant Pan Tao said to Jie: 'Your talents, learning, and reasoning are sufficient to untie the two gentlemen's quarrel; you may try to discuss it.'
s0394.idiomatic: Pan Tao urged Wang Jie that his scholarship could settle the feud between Wei Heng's and Wang Tingjian's schools.

s0395.literal: Jie thereupon set out in detail their strengths and weaknesses.
s0395.idiomatic: Wang Jie then weighed each side's strengths and flaws in full detail.

s0396.literal: Zhi Yu and Xie Heng both broadly comprehended and broadly heard; all thought it appropriate.
s0396.idiomatic: Zhi Yu and Xie Heng, both celebrated polymaths, judged his verdict sound.

s0397.literal: Also he compiled Continued Biographies of Exemplary Women seventy-two persons, miscellaneous discourses, rhapsodies, stele eulogics, and refutations over one hundred thousand graphs; in mourning turmoil all was lost.
s0397.idiomatic: He also wrote seventy-two further exemplary women's lives and well over a hundred thousand characters of essays, verse, inscriptions, and polemics—all lost in the wars.

s0398.literal: The eldest son Qianqi drifted lodged south of the river; following his father's original intent, he again annotated Gongyang, and also gathered Continued Biographies of Exemplary Women.
s0398.idiomatic: His eldest son Qianqi, exiled south of the Yangzi, re-edited the Gongyang commentary in his father's spirit and reassembled the sequel to Exemplary Women.

s0400.literal: The court historian says: Huangfu Mi in plain tread was darkly chaste; idle residence nurtured illness; he placed feeling in brush-cutting; earnestly delighted in mounds and tombs; tall caps and tethered ribbons were not enough to be glory; poverty and low status he did not take as shame; firmly unmoved—thus is he indeed a lofty man of Jin!
s0400.idiomatic: The historians praise Huangfu Mi for living plainly in seclusion, tending chronic illness while devoting himself to scholarship; rank could not tempt him and want could not shame him—an unbending Jin exemplar of the first rank.

s0401.literal: Down to when Sincere to the End set up argument, thin burial illuminated frugality; already warning luxury in the Ji clan, also having nothing to take from Prince Yang of Wei; it can be called grasping the pivot of survival and death.
s0401.idiomatic: His essay Sincere to the End preached modest burial, warning against the Jis' extravagance without copying Yang Wangsun's naked interment—altogether a balanced grasp of how to meet mortality.
